newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/mark ends US higher as euro concerns mount.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark ends US higher as euro concerns mount.

text.p: *Dlr pushes to higher close vs mark after touching near one-month intraday top of 1.7320. Ends little changed vs yen.
*Mark slumps broadly after French left victory prompts doubts over future euro's strength. EMU resolve still seen strong.
*Dlr/mark 3-yr peak of 1.7389 within reach if US data firm.
*Safe-haven dollar buying to continue as EMU debate intensifies.

The dollar added to massive overseas gains against a broadly weak mark on Monday, pushing up to near one-month highs against the German currency after French elections raised questions about the strength of Europe's planned single currency.

French voters resoundingly rejected outgoing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's policies of fiscal austerity on Sunday, sweeping Socialist leader Lionel Jospin into office and signalling a shift in France's push to meet strict Maastricht criteria for monetary union.

While supportive of Europe's drive to create a single currency, Jospin -- and French voters for that matter -- have made it clear that they will not tolerate further economic sacrifice in meeting EMU guidelines.
As a result, dealers fled to the safe-haven of dollars, betting that the euro would evolve into a much weaker currency than originally envisioned.

"It looks like Europe will go ahead with EMU, but it also looks like the euro will be much weaker than people had expected," said Robert Sabia, vice president on the foreign exchange desk at ING Barings Capital Markets.

The dollar ended at 1.7290/00 marks, up from 1.7265/75 at the open and sharply higher than Friday's close of 1.7050/60. In the early afternoon, it reached a session high of 1.7320, its top rate since early May.

The mark, which has the most to lose from the introduction of a weak euro, slumped against a host of other currencies as well, ending near session lows versus the yen, sterling, the Italian lira and the Spanish peseta. Although speculation of a delay in the EMU timetable circulated in the market, traders said market action reflected a belief that political resolve to push through the plan, as scheduled, remained strong.
"There has been so much political capital invested in this, I just don't think they can stop the wheels at this point," said John Beerling, chief dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
Traders said the French election results had diverted some attention away from an ongoing row between the German government and the Bundesbank over plans to revalue gold reserves.
But they said recent developments pointed to additional safe-haven buying of dollars in the weeks and months to come as debate over monetary union heats up.

"Given the mess that the euro debate is going to create in Europe ... the best place to look is out of town," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York. "The dollar will be the prime beneficiary of that."
Dealers pegged near-term resistance in dollar/mark at 1.7350, with a stronger hurdle near its late-April peak of 1.7389.
Against the yen, the dollar stuck to an extremely tight range in U.S. trade on Monday, ending at 116.55/65 versus 116.62/67 at the open.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.4320/30 Swiss francs from 1.4350/60 at the open, but remained well above its Friday closing rate of 1.4140/50.
Sterling, which was another beneficiary of mark weakness on Monday, pushed up to $1.6362/72 by the close against $1.6315/25 at the open.
The dollar weakened to Canadian $1.3735/40 from C$1.3762/67, while the Australian dollar slumped to $0.7567/72 from $0.7600/05 at the open.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
